question.text: A risk tolerance questionnaire presents two versions of the same scenario to a client: Version A says "In this investment, 10 out of 100 investors lost money." Version B says "In this investment, 90 out of 100 investors made money." The client shows higher risk appetite with Version B. This is an example of:

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook defines framing bias as people answering differently based on how facts are presented, and uses the same 10-out-of-100-loss versus 90-out-of-100-save style example. The workbook also notes that framing can affect responses to risk-tolerance questionnaires, which is exactly what is happening with the client here. The Trap: Anchoring bias involves fixating on a specific reference number rather than reacting to a positive versus negative frame. Stereotype bias and choice paralysis describe different mechanisms and do not fit the gain-frame versus loss-frame contrast. Note: The workbook stresses that risk-profiling questionnaires must be fair, clear and not misleading; framing preference can be diagnosed with the right tools and then reconfirmed through client discussion before relying on the score.
